nameStory: The "superb" jewelwing earned its regal name from the male's absolutely stunning metallic green body that shimmers like an emerald in sunlight. All jewelwings get their name from their jewel-like coloration and broad, iridescent wings that catch light like precious gems dancing over water.
description: The Superb Jewelwing is a broad-winged damselfly that's about 2 inches long from head to tail. Males are dazzling metallic green creatures with amber-tinted wings, while females have a more subdued bronze body with greenish wings tipped in white. Unlike their thin-winged cousins, jewelwings have notably wide wings that they hold out perpendicular to their bodies when at rest, making them easy to spot along streams and rivers.

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: Wings held straight out from the body when perched, not folded back like most damselflies - they look like tiny helicopters ready for takeoff

idTips.label: Male Coloration
idTips.description: Males shine like polished emeralds with brilliant metallic green bodies that seem to glow in dappled sunlight, paired with amber-washed wings

idTips.label: Female Appearance
idTips.description: Females are more muted with bronze-tinged bodies and greenish wings marked with distinctive white tips that flash when they fly

idTips.label: Wing Width
idTips.description: Wings are notably broad and substantial-looking compared to typical damselflies - they feel almost butterfly-like in their width

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: About 2 inches long, making them among the larger damselflies you'll encounter in New England waterways

habitat: Look for Superb Jewelwings along clear, flowing rivers and streams with good vegetation nearby - they need clean water to thrive. They prefer areas where trees and shrubs overhang the water, creating dappled light conditions perfect for spotting their metallic shimmer. You'll often find them sharing habitat with clubtail dragonflies in these pristine waterways.

seasonality.spring: Not yet active - nymphs are still developing underwater in the stream bottom, feeding on small aquatic insects.
seasonality.summer: Peak season! Adults emerge in June and July, when males establish territories along streams and their metallic bodies are most vibrant in the warm sunlight.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down by late summer, though you might spot a few stragglers in early fall before they complete their lifecycle.
seasonality.winter: Only nymphs are present, hidden underwater among rocks and debris, slowly growing through the cold months.

funFact: Male Superb Jewelwings are such dedicated territory holders that they'll chase away not just other jewelwings, but also much larger dragonflies, butterflies, and even small birds that dare to fly through their claimed stretch of stream - talk about punching above your weight class!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Ebony Jewelwing, but males are key: Superb males are brilliant metallic green while Ebony males are darker with more black coloration. Remember: "Superb = Super-green" for the males' distinctive emerald shine.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "damselflies," these insects are fierce predators both as adults and underwater nymphs. The "damsel" name is misleading - there's nothing delicate about their hunting prowess, though they are more slender than their dragonfly cousins.
compareHints: Superb Jewelwings are distinguished from other New England jewelwings primarily by the male's bright metallic green body color. Ebony Jewelwing males are much darker with black bodies, while River Jewelwings have more blue-green coloration. The Sparkling Jewelwing is less common and has different wing patterns with less amber coloration.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the jewelwing species, Ebony Jewelwings are the only ones where males have completely black wings - River Jewelwings have metallic green wing patches, Sparkling Jewelwings have wings that are only partly darkened, and Superb Jewelwings show brilliant blue-green iridescence.
River Jewelwings can be distinguished from Ebony Jewelwings by their preference for larger waterways and slightly different wing coloration patterns.
Compared to the Ebony Jewelwing, the Sparkling Jewelwing has more extensive metallic green-blue coloration on both wings and body, while Ebony Jewelwings are generally darker overall.
